school: Social Psychology, Attribution Theory, Interpersonal Relations
legacy: Harold Kelley is remembered as one of the most influential social psychologists of the twentieth century. His work helped explain how people interpret behavior, assign causes to events, and form judgments about others. By developing systematic theories of social reasoning, he contributed to a deeper understanding of everyday decision-making, relationships, and human interaction. His ideas continue to shape research in psychology, communication, education, and behavioral sciences.
earlyLife: Kelley developed an early interest in human behavior, learning, and scientific inquiry. During his education, he became fascinated by the processes through which people understand one another and make sense of social situations. These interests directed him toward psychology and eventually toward the study of social perception, interpersonal relationships, and human judgment.
scientificField: Psychology, Social Psychology, Interpersonal Relations, Cognitive Science
majorContributions: Kelley made foundational contributions to attribution theory, which examines how individuals explain the causes of actions and events. He proposed that people act as informal investigators, gathering information and evaluating evidence when interpreting behavior. His covariation model explained how consistency, distinctiveness, and consensus influence judgments about causation. Kelley also conducted influential research on close relationships, cooperation, attraction, commitment, and social exchange. His work helped establish modern relationship science and provided valuable insights into how people understand and navigate social life.
laterLife: During the later stages of his career, Kelley continued refining theories of interpersonal behavior and social cognition. He collaborated with researchers studying relationships, motivation, and social influence, helping expand the scientific investigation of human interaction. His later writings emphasized the importance of understanding both individual thought processes and the broader social environments in which people operate.
whyImportant: Harold Kelley is important because he helped explain how people construct explanations for behavior and how those explanations influence relationships, judgments, and decisions. His theories provided powerful tools for understanding social perception and interpersonal dynamics. Modern research on relationships, social cognition, organizational behavior, and communication continues to draw upon concepts he helped develop.
